approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would shut down the Energy Efficiency Opportunities program from 29 June 2014.
It would repeal the Energy Efficiency Opportunities Act 2006, which currently requires large energy users to assess and report on energy savings.
If the bill becomes law after 29 June 2014, the repeal would apply retrospectively from that date.
Terminates the Energy Efficiency Opportunities program on 29 June 2014.
Repeals the Energy Efficiency Opportunities Act 2006.
Provides that repeal may be retrospective if royal assent occurs after 29 June 2014.
Large energy-using businesses that consume over 0.5 petajoules annually and medium energy-users that participate voluntarily.

Lisa Singh This Energy Efficiency Opportunities (Repeal) Bill 2014 before us is another example of this government's repealing of a once bipartisan effective piece of legislation introduced by the Howard government to enable Australia to deal with this century's inevitable transformation of energy generation and supply. Its repeal is another irrevocable and incredible indication that this coalition government is more reactionary and owns less foresight than the Howard government, characteristics which many of us might not have thought possible back in 2007. But just like the Renewable Energy Target, the energy efficiency opportunities legislation is being repealed because it was too successful. Energy efficiency refers to gaining the same or higher level of useful output using less energy input. Increased energy efficiency is a very effective economic driver. It reduces overall demand for energy and delays the need for new energy generation equipment. Energy efficiency is also about productivity. It is about lower inputs and bigger outputs. It is about lower costs and doing things better, doing things smarter and doing things more cost-effectively. Improving Australia's uptake of commercial energy efficiency opportunities has the potential to increase our economic health and lower the rate of growth in greenhouse gas emissions. In 2004, along with the Labor Party, the Howard government recognised that bipartisan energy policy action was needed. The energy white paper in June 2004 entitled _Securing Australia's energy future_ identified the improvement of Australia's energy-efficiency performance as a key part of the Howard government's energy policy in order to achieve greater prosperity, sustainability and energy security. The Energy Efficiency Opportunities Bill 2005 was to establish the mandatory energy efficiency opportunities assessments announced in that white paper. Introduced the Energy Efficiency Opportunities (Repeal) Bill 2014, arguing the mandatory energy-assessment scheme for large users had become superfluous as businesses already manage energy costs, and that repeal, backdated to 29 June 2014, would save Australian businesses $17.7 million a year.

Argued that the Energy Efficiency Opportunities program, introduced by the Howard government in 2006, has saved industry approximately $323.2 million a year in power expenses for a compliance cost of just $17 million across 464 companies, and said Labor will not block its repeal but questioned the logic of scrapping a program that delivers such returns.

Argued in support of repealing the Energy Efficiency Opportunities program as an outdated regulatory burden now that businesses manage energy efficiently by habit, noting South Australian electricity bills have risen 160 per cent under the state Labor government, and said the carbon tax, currently $24.15 a tonne and rising to $38 a tonne by 2019, cost the economy over $6 billion in its first year.

Opposed the repeal, criticising the government's climate stance while noting the United States has cut greenhouse gas emissions by around 17 per cent and China is rolling out emissions trading schemes covering some 250 million people, and said Australia's Renewable Energy Target has created about 24,000 jobs that this government is undermining.

Opposed the repeal, citing a GLOBE Climate Legislation Study of 66 countries finding Australia is the only one taking negative climate policy action, referenced IPCC warnings that emissions must fall 40 to 70 per cent from 2010 levels by 2050, and warned that a collapsing West Antarctic ice sheet could eventually raise sea levels by up to four metres.

Opposed the repeal, noting Australian and German scientists recently discovered a new chemical element, No. 117, and questioned why the government ignores such scientific expertise on climate change, citing the Energy Efficiency Council's finding that every dollar invested in the program delivered $2.90 in benefits against savings of $323.2 million a year.

Argued in support of repealing the Energy Efficiency Opportunities Act, noting Australia has 111 years of black coal supply and 539 years of brown coal, disputed climate alarm by citing 767,000 square kilometres of additional Antarctic sea ice compared with the 1981 to 2000 average, and said the carbon tax costs households in Parramatta $550 a year.

Argued that the previous speaker's climate change denial ignores the fact that 97 per cent of published scientific papers conclude climate change is real and man-made, with scientists now expressing 95 per cent certainty, comparable to the certainty that tobacco causes cancer.

Opposed repealing the Energy Efficiency Opportunities Act, saying an independent review found it saved companies over $800 million a year in energy costs, and criticised the Emissions Reduction Fund's budget allocation of $1.1 billion as falling well short of the $2.55 billion the environment minister had promised.

Supported repealing the Energy Efficiency Opportunities Act, saying it will save Australian businesses $17.7 million a year in compliance costs while businesses will still save $323 million annually on energy costs through practices now standard across industry, and said the government is investing $1 billion in ARENA funding across nearly 200 renewable energy projects.
